subject: zoology
question_text: What is predation? Give an example.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.62, VSAQ 172). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. WORDING: the book defines predation as 'a feeding strategy ... in which predator gets benefited at the cost of the prey'. The word strategy suggests a plan, so this card states the event instead — the predator kills and eats the prey (Rule 41, plain literal language).

steps.why: Predation differs from parasitism in one fact: the prey is killed, not merely harmed. The book calls predation a 'feeding strategy'; this card writes what happens instead, because the mark is for the interaction and not for a plan.
common_mistakes: Writing that the prey is harmed. In predation the prey is KILLED.
Writing that the predator lives on the prey. That describes a parasite.
steps.memory_tip: Parasite harms and stays; predator kills and leaves.
steps.margin_note: One sentence naming the predator and the prey, then one line on who gains.

steps.label: Example

lines.text: The predator kills, the prey is eaten

lines: Ex: the lion (predator) and the deer (prey).
Predation keeps the number of prey animals
steps.why: The example is short, so the space left goes to the ecological value of predation, which is the extra point that lifts a one-line answer to two marks.
common_mistakes: Giving Plasmodium in man. That is parasitism, because the host is not killed outright.
Naming the two animals without saying which is which.
steps.memory_tip: Say the pair with the roles attached: lion is the predator, deer is the prey.
steps.margin_note: Name the pair with roles marked, then one line on population control.

insider_note: Mark the roles beside the names — lion (predator), deer (prey) — because an unlabelled pair can be read either way.
